title: The breath you already have

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last story: Holi, Kama burned to ash, and love set loose without a body. Your line was everyone's the same color today. The stories are behind us. Camp three begins. Day ninety-seven.

Welcome to camp three: the practices. For the next nine weeks, less listening and more doing. Each week adds one piece to a routine that's yours. And we start with the one thing you've been doing, without a break, since the second you were born. You're doing it now. Twenty thousand times a day or so, you breathe in and out, and almost none of those breaths are ones you chose. You don't decide to breathe while you sleep. You don't decide while you read this. It just happens. The tradition has a word for what's moving when it does.
screen: `CAMP THREE: THE PRACTICES.` → `SINCE THE SECOND YOU WERE BORN.` → `YOU DON'T DECIDE IT.`

segments.voice: The word is prana. It's often translated as breath, and it is breath, but it's more than air. Prana means life, the life-force, the thing that's moving in you as long as you're alive. The breath is where you can feel it most easily. The Upanishads, among the oldest texts of the tradition, tell a story about it. The senses have an argument about which of them is most important. Speech says: me. The eye says: me. The ear, the mind: me, me. So they agree to a test. Each one leaves the body for a year. Speech leaves, and the body lives on, silent. The eye leaves, and the body lives on, blind. The ear, the mind, the same. Then breath gets ready to leave. And, the Chandogya Upanishad says, like a strong horse tearing up the pegs it's tied to, it starts to pull all the others up with it. They beg it to stay. You're the greatest, they say. Don't go. That's the idea behind this whole week. Everything else you do, you do because breath is doing its work first. So pranayama, the breath practices, doesn't begin by controlling anything. It begins by noticing. Just watching the breath that's already here, without changing it. That's harder than it sounds, because the moment you watch it, you'll want to fix it. Don't. Let it be the way it is. Here's the turn: you don't breathe. It breathes you.
screen: `PRANA — BREATH, AND LIFE ITSELF.` · `THE SENSES ARGUE.` · `BREATH TEARS UP THE PEGS.` · `FIRST, JUST NOTICE.` · then, large: `IT BREATHES YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch the breath. Sit comfortably, back tall but not stiff. Let your hands rest. Close your eyes, or lower them. Now, find the breath. Where do you feel it most? The cool air at the tip of the nose. The rise of the chest. The belly moving. Pick one place and rest your attention there. Don't deepen the breath. Don't slow it. Just watch it come in, and go out, the way you'd watch waves. When your mind wanders, and it will, that's fine. Notice where it went, and come back to the breath. Every coming back is the practice. The bell holds the time.
Prana. Breath, and the life that moves with it. The first thing the practice asks you to notice.
Your line: it breathes you. Three times today, at a red light, in a line, before you open an email, catch one breath, just one, and notice it happening on its own. Day ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Many Hindus begin daily meditation or puja by sitting quietly and watching the breath for a few minutes, understood as prana, the life-force, before any breath practice or mantra.

original.note: Sanskrit: breath, and the life-force it carries.

trapdoor: what you thought: prana is a yoga word for deep breathing.
what it means: breath, and the life that moves in you; the practice starts by watching it, not steering it.
what a scholar hears: the contest of the senses in the Chandogya and Brihadaranyaka Upanishads, where breath proves itself the chief of the vital powers.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 5.1.6–5.1.12 (the contest of the senses; the horse and its pegs)

notes: The contest of the senses: Chandogya 5.1 lists speech, eye, ear, mind; breath is compared to a fine horse tearing up its tethering pegs (5.1.12). Paraphrased. Confirm verse numbers.
'Twenty thousand times a day or so': adult resting rate of 12–20 breaths per minute gives roughly 17,000–29,000; traditional yoga texts give 21,600. Confirm or soften.
